title: Standard check-ups for children and teenagers in Germany
intro: In Germany, children and teenagers are offered a series of preventive check-ups at set ages, paid for by health insurance. They monitor growth and development, detect problems early, and offer parents the chance to ask questions. This article gives a general overview; schedules are updated from time to time, so check details with your paediatrician.

sections.heading: Why check-ups matter
paragraphs: Regular check-ups find conditions such as hearing and vision problems, developmental delay, growth disorders and feeding difficulties early, when support works best. They also provide a regular opportunity to discuss sleep, nutrition, behaviour, safety and the child's wellbeing, and to review vaccinations.

sections.heading: Check-ups in early childhood
paragraphs: Newborns are examined right after birth and again in the first weeks. Further check-ups follow in the first year at several set times, then in the second, third and fourth years and before school entry. They include measuring height and weight, examining organs, assessing movement, language and social skills, hearing and vision checks, and advice for parents. The numbered check-ups are known as the U examinations.

sections.heading: Check-ups for older children and teenagers
paragraphs: Additional check-ups take place in later childhood and adolescence, with a focus on school performance, mental health, puberty, nutrition, screen use and risk behaviours. Teenagers have a check-up in early adolescence, the J1, with a further one offered later in some regions or by some insurers.

sections.heading: Dental and other services
paragraphs: Regular dental check-ups begin in the first years of life. Vaccinations are recommended according to the national schedule and may be given at these visits. Hearing screening for newborns and vision screening are also part of care.

sections.heading: The yellow booklet
paragraphs: Results are recorded in the child's examination booklet, commonly called the yellow booklet, which should be kept safe together with the vaccination record. Bring it to every visit and when moving or travelling. Keep appointments, and ask your paediatrician if you have missed one. Counselling is available for families with concerns.

examples.title: Preparing for a visit
examples.text: Imagine your child has a check-up next week. You could write down questions about sleep, eating and behaviour and bring the yellow booklet and vaccination record.

examples.title: Catching up
examples.text: Suppose you moved and missed a check-up. You might contact a paediatric practice, explain the situation and ask whether the missed check-up can still be done.
